definition: In computer science, learning vector quantization (LVQ) is a prototype-based supervised classification algorithm.
details: LVQ is the supervised counterpart of vector quantization systems. LVQ can be understood as a special case of an artificial neural network, more precisely, it applies a winner-take-all Hebbian learning-based approach. It is a precursor to self-organizing maps (SOM) and related to neural gas and the k-nearest neighbor algorithm (k-NN). LVQ was invented by Teuvo Kohonen.

explainer.lead: Learning vector quantization classifies data using labelled prototypes that are moved during training. It matters as a simple, interpretable classifier and as a historical bridge to self-organizing maps.

tiers.eli5: It is like placing labelled landmarks on a map and then moving each landmark toward the examples it should represent, so new points are classed by the nearest landmark.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers keep a set of labelled prototype vectors and use a winner-take-all update: the closest prototype is pulled toward correctly classified inputs and pushed away from misclassified ones. A pitfall is that results depend heavily on prototype initialization and on the choice of distance metric.
tiers.paperLevel: A special case of an artificial neural network applying winner-take-all, Hebbian-style learning, related to self-organizing maps, neural gas and k-nearest neighbour; classification assigns an input to its nearest prototype's class. Performance hinges on prototype count and initialization, and it suits prototype-shaped class structure.

explainer.example: A digit-recognition task keeps one prototype per digit; a new image is assigned to whichever prototype is closest after training moves each prototype toward its own examples.
